course.title: Logic and Reasoning
course.description: Work out what follows from what. Read arguments carefully, test them against cases, and see where everyday reasoning goes wrong.
course.audience: A general reader with no background in formal logic who wants to argue and evaluate arguments more carefully.

paragraphs: How can you tell whether a conclusion really follows from the reasons given for it? Logic is the study of that question, and it gives you ways of answering it that don't depend on how convincing an argument sounds. It helps you read arguments more carefully and see where everyday reasoning goes wrong, and it is also the rule-following side of mathematics and computing.

The ways it gives are checks you can carry out. Every claim is true or false, so a few claims can only come out in a limited number of combinations, and a question about them can be settled by going through the combinations one at a time. An if-then rule is broken in exactly one of four cases, for instance, and an argument is valid when no combination makes its reasons true and its conclusion false.

The most useful distinction it draws is between whether a conclusion follows and whether the reasons are true. An argument can follow perfectly from a false premise, and one whose premises are all true can still fail to support its conclusion, so keeping the two questions apart shows you what to challenge in a conclusion you reject.
outcomes: You'll be able to tell a claim from a question or a command, and say what its truth value is.
You'll be able to say exactly when an if-then rule is broken, and write its converse and its contrapositive.
You'll be able to solve a knights and knaves puzzle by trying each case and ruling out the ones that break a rule.
You'll be able to build a truth table for two claims and use it to test a piece of reasoning.
You'll be able to pick out the conclusion of an argument, tell valid from sound, and name the common fallacies.
introduction.prerequisites: You don't need any background in logic or mathematics, only the habit of reading a sentence carefully.

lessons.title: What logic operates on

lead.text: Sort the sentences you meet by what they are doing and three kinds come out. Some say how things are, such as “The lamp is on”. Some ask, as in “Is the door locked?”, and some tell, as in “Switch the lamp on”. We call a sentence of the first kind a **claim**, and the test for one is whether it can be *wrong*.

afterFigure.text: Only a claim puts forward **something the world can contradict**, and that is why logic, which is about what follows from what we put forward, works on claims and leaves the other two kinds alone.
The test has nothing to do with whether we agree or can check: “The lamp is on” is a claim whether or not the lamp is on, and whether or not you can see it from where you are.

lead.text: The sentence “The envelope holds a £10 note” hasn't been checked, but that doesn't leave it in some third state of being neither right nor wrong. The envelope holds a note or it doesn't, and whichever it is has already settled the sentence. Open the envelope each way in the figure and see what happens to it, and to its opposite, “The envelope holds no £10 note”.

afterFigure.text: Whichever way the envelope goes, one sentence is true and the other false. We call *true* or *false* a claim's **truth value**, and in this course every claim has exactly one of the two. “Unknown” is not a third value, because it describes you, who haven't looked, and not the sentence.
In every such case, such as a claim about the past that no one can now check, **the facts fix the truth value**, and whether we have found it out is a separate matter.

lead.text: The two sentences in the envelope figure are linked in a way that is worth naming. “The envelope holds no £10 note” says exactly what you would need to say to deny the first, and we call a claim that denies another claim its **negation**. We write the negation of a claim p as ¬p, read “not p”, so if p is “The lamp is on”, then ¬p is “The lamp is not on”.
Negating a claim reverses its truth value: **if p is true then ¬p is false, and if p is false then ¬p is true**.

afterFigure.text: Take care that a negation denies the claim and nothing more. The negation of “The soup is hot” is “The soup is not hot”, which leaves room for the soup being merely warm, and it is *not* “The soup is cold”.

reveal.text: Each row of the table sets a value of p beside the value of ¬p, and in both rows the two differ. Cold soup is not hot, so p is false here and ¬p is true.

lead.text: So far the claims have been ones you could settle by looking. Many sentences that people argue over are not like that, such as “Cats make better pets than dogs” or “The new tax is unfair”. It is tempting to say that these are only opinions, neither true nor false, and so none of logic's business.

But someone who says the tax is unfair is putting something forward as *how things are*, and someone who answers “No, it isn't” is contradicting it. **Being a claim doesn't depend on our agreeing, or even on our knowing how to settle it**; it depends only on the sentence being put forward as true, so that it can be doubted.

Whether some claims, about taste or fairness for example, have a truth value at all is a hard question in philosophy, and logic doesn't need the answer, because it asks what follows *if* the claim is true and what follows if it is false.

blocks.text: Here is a sentence: “The envelope on the table holds a £10 note.” The envelope is sealed and nobody has looked inside, so we can't say whether the sentence is right. It will be shown to be right or wrong the moment someone looks, which we can't say of “Does the envelope hold a £10 note?” or “Open the envelope.”
Logic asks what follows from what, and it can only work on sentences that can be *right or wrong*, since a question has nothing to be wrong about and a command can only be obeyed or ignored.

recap.keyIdea: A claim is a sentence that can be wrong, it has one truth value whether or not anyone knows it, and its negation takes the opposite value.

blocks.text: A **claim** says how things are, so unlike a question or a command it can turn out to be wrong, even when people dispute it. Each claim has one of two **truth values**, true or false, and the facts settle which *whether or not* anyone has looked. Its **negation**, ¬p, says the opposite, and so always takes the other value.

lessons.title: If-then claims

lead.text: The lock's rule is built out of two shorter [[claims|Sentences that say how things are, so they can turn out to be wrong. Met in 'What logic operates on'.]], “The access code is correct” and “The door opens”, and we call a claim built this way a **conditional**. The part after “if” is its **antecedent**, the part after “then” is its **consequent**, and if we let p stand for the first and q for the second we can write the whole thing as p → q, read “if p then q”.

afterFigure.text: The “then” is often dropped and the order often swapped. “The door opens if the code is correct” says exactly what the lock's rule says, because **the antecedent is whatever follows “if”**, wherever it stands in the sentence.

diagram.alt: Two boxes joined by an arrow. The left box is p, the antecedent: the access code is correct. The right box is q, the consequent: the door opens. Together they read p → q.
diagram.caption: The rule as a conditional: the arrow points from the condition to what is said to follow.

lead.text: Take the two things that can happen once the code has been entered correctly. If the door opens, the rule has done its job. If the door stays shut, the rule has been broken, and the claim “If the code is correct, the door opens” is *false*.

afterFigure.text: So a conditional is false when **its antecedent is true and its consequent is false**, because that is a case where the rule demands something and doesn't get it.

diagram.caption: The code is right in both pictures. Only the door differs, and only one of the two breaks the rule.

reveal.text: With the letters this way round the lock's rule is q → p. The table lists all four combinations, and only the third row, with p false and q true, is one where it comes out false: the code is correct and the door stays shut.
The rule said what happens when the code is correct and nothing else, so a shut door after a wrong code contradicts nothing it said.

lead.text: The pull to call that case false comes from reading the rule as a claim about the door in general. “If the code is correct, the door opens” tells us what happens in one situation, when the code is right, and it stays quiet about every other. With a wrong code the door can stay shut, or it can open because someone inside presses the release button, and neither contradicts what the rule says.

afterFigure.text: In both pictures the antecedent is false, so the rule was never put to the test. Nothing has broken it, and we count the conditional as **true whenever its antecedent is false**, whatever the consequent does. That is a convention, but it is the right one for a rule: a rule that hasn't been broken has been kept, and the conditional stays a claim with a definite [[truth value|True or false: the one verdict a claim has. Met in 'What logic operates on'.]].

lead.text: Each of p and q can be true or false, which gives four combinations, and the conditional is false in exactly one of them, where p is true and q is false. A list of this kind, which sets out every case and the value the claim takes in each, is called a **truth table**.

afterFigure.text: A conditional never asserts that p is true, and it doesn't assert that p *causes* q, only that p without q is ruled out. Whenever you meet an if-then claim, **look for the one case it forbids**.

blocks.text: Take the rule “If the access code is correct, the door opens.” It is easy to say what breaks it: the right code is typed and the door stays shut. It is harder to say what the rule claims about a wrong code, since it never mentions one.
Rules of this form run through laws, instructions and the premises of arguments, so the first thing to settle about one is how much it claims.

intro.promise: By the end you'll name the parts of an if-then claim, say when it is false, and judge it when its condition fails.
intro.whyItMatters: Most rules, laws and arguments are if-then claims, and most mistakes about them come from misreading when they fail.

recap.keyIdea: A conditional p → q is false only when p is true and q is false, and true in every other case.

blocks.text: An **if-then claim** joins an antecedent p to a consequent q, and the arrow points from the condition to what is said to follow. It forbids exactly *one* case, p true with q false, so it is true in the other three, including both in which p is false, because a rule whose condition never arises has not been broken.

recap.nextHook: Next we turn a conditional round, and find that one way of doing it changes what it says and another doesn't.

lessons.title: Converse and contrapositive

lead.text: The simplest way to turn the lock's [[conditional|An if-then claim, p → q. It is false only when p is true and q is false. Met in 'If-then claims'.]] p → q round is to swap its [[antecedent|The part of a conditional after “if”: the condition. Met in 'If-then claims'.]] and its [[consequent|The part of a conditional after “then”: what is said to follow. Met in 'If-then claims'.]], which gives q → p, or in words “If the door opens, the code is correct”. We call the claim we get by swapping the two parts the **converse** of the original.

afterFigure.text: The converse is made of *exactly the same material* as the original, so it is easy to hear it as just another way of saying the same thing. **Whether two conditionals say the same thing has to be checked case by case**, as we did for the conditional itself.

diagram.caption: The rule, and the claim made by swapping its two halves. The swapped claim is the converse.

lead.text: How do we decide whether two claims say the same thing? Not by how alike their wording is, but by whether they can *ever* disagree. If there is a case in which one is true and the other false, they are different claims, and if there is no such case, they are the same as far as logic is concerned. So we check them one case at a time. The figure begins the check for p → q and its converse q → p, with a row for each combination of p and q, and in the first row, where both are true, p → q is true and so is q → p.

afterFigure.text: One row of agreement settles nothing, because two quite different claims can agree in some rows. **One row of disagreement settles everything**, because it shows that the two can come apart. We should therefore go looking for such a row, and the natural place to start is where p and q have different values.

diagram.caption: To compare two claims, check them row by row. The first row is done, and the two agree in it.

reveal.text: In this row q → p is false, while p → q is true because its antecedent is false. The two disagree, so the converse is a *different* claim from the original.

lead.text: Swap the parts as before, and then [[negate|To make the claim that denies another, written ¬p. It reverses the truth value. Met in 'What logic operates on'.]] each of them. The result is ¬q → ¬p, read “if not q then not p”, which in words is “If the door does not open, the code is not correct”. We call it the **contrapositive** of p → q.

afterFigure.text: *Both* steps are needed. Negating without swapping gives ¬p → ¬q, “If the code is not correct, the door does not open”, which is neither the [[converse|The conditional with its parts swapped: q → p. Met earlier in this lesson.]] nor the contrapositive. The contrapositive is the one that **swaps and negates**.

steps.headline: Does the contrapositive ever disagree with the original?

lead.text: The rows will tell us. For each combination of p and q we work out p → q first and ¬q → ¬p second, and the values are written in that order.

workedSteps.text: Take p true and q true. Then p → q is true. In the contrapositive ¬q is false, so its antecedent is false and ¬q → ¬p is true as well.
Take p true and q false. Now p → q has a true antecedent and a false consequent, so it is false, and the contrapositive ¬q → ¬p comes out false as well.
Take p false and q true. Then p → q is true, because its antecedent is false. Here ¬q is false, so the contrapositive's antecedent is false and it is true too.
Take p false and q false. Then p → q is true. Now ¬q and ¬p are both true, so ¬q → ¬p has a true antecedent and a true consequent, and it is true.
In all four rows the two claims take the same value, so there is no case in which they can disagree. The contrapositive says the same thing as the original.

lead.text: The practical gain is that the contrapositive gives us a second way of using a rule we already hold. Because “If the code is correct, the door opens” and “If the door does not open, the code is not correct” say the same thing, we may take the rule together with a door that stayed shut and conclude that the code was wrong. The conclusion is exactly as safe as the rule itself.

The converse offers no such service. From an open door we would like to say that the code was right, but that needs the rule “If the door opens, the code is correct”, which the manual *never* gave us and which can be false while the manual's rule is true. So from the original rule and an open door **nothing follows about the code**.

lessons.orientation: The converse and the contrapositive of an if-then claim, and which one says the same as the original.
lessons.nextAction: Next, a puzzle solved by trying each case in turn.

blocks.text: Take the rule in a lock's manual, “If the access code is correct, the door opens”, and turn it round. Swapping its two halves gives “If the door opens, the code is correct”, and swapping them and negating each gives “If the door does not open, the code is not correct”. Both are built from the same two parts as the rule, and each can sound like the rule said in other words, so it is fair to ask whether either really is.

The question matters because we reason backwards from rules all the time, from a shut door to a wrong code or from an open door to a right one, and of those two moves one is safe and one is not. Working out which turnings of a rule say the same as the rule, and which say something new, is what lets you tell the safe move from the unsafe one.

intro.promise: By the end you'll write the converse and contrapositive of an if-then claim, and say which one means the same as the original.
intro.whyItMatters: Reasoning from a rule in the wrong direction is one of the commonest errors in argument, and turning the rule round correctly avoids it.

recap.keyIdea: Swapping a conditional's parts gives its converse, which can disagree with it; swapping and negating both gives its contrapositive, which always agrees.

blocks.text: The **converse** of p → q is q → p, and it is a different claim, since the two split in two of the four cases. The **contrapositive**, ¬q → ¬p, swaps the parts *and* negates both, and it takes the same value as the original in every case, so a rule can be used backwards through its contrapositive but never through its converse.

lessons.title: Knights and knaves

lead.text: On the island in these puzzles everyone is one of two kinds. A **knight** always tells the truth, so every sentence a knight says is true, and a **knave** always lies, so every sentence a knave says is false.

afterFigure.text: The rule works in both directions: if we know that what someone said is false, we know they can't be a knight, so they must be a knave. The rule is about the [[truth value|True or false: the one verdict a claim has. Met in 'What logic operates on'.]] of what is said, so a knave may say something long and complicated, as long as it *comes out false*.

lead.text: Suppose an islander called Cleo says of another, Dan, “Dan is a knight.” We try each possibility in turn and see what it forces. If Cleo is a knight, her sentence is true, so Dan is a knight. If Cleo is a knave, her sentence is false, so Dan must be a knave, and again nothing has gone wrong.

afterFigure.text: Neither assumption breaks a rule, so Cleo's sentence doesn't settle *what* she is. What it does settle is *how* she and Dan are related, since in both cases they are the same kind, and that is the usual shape of these puzzles: **one statement narrows the possibilities without picking one**.

lead.text: With two islanders, each a knight or a knave, there are four ways the island might be arranged: both knights, both knaves, and the two mixed pairs. We call a choice of kind for every person an **assignment**, and the plan is to write all of them down and test each against what has been said, such as Cleo's “Dan is a knight”.

afterFigure.text: Two assignments fail. Where Cleo is a knight and Dan a knave, the knight has said something *false*, and where Cleo is a knave and Dan a knight, the knave has said something *true*. Each of these needs a sentence to be true and false at once, and a situation like that is a **contradiction**, so we rule the assignment out. What is left, an assignment in which nobody breaks the rule for their kind, is a possible answer, and **a puzzle is solved when exactly one assignment is left**.

steps.headline: Eli says “Fay and I are the same kind”, and Fay says “Eli is a knave”

lead.text: Here is a puzzle solved in full, with every assignment tested against both statements.

workedSteps.text: Four assignments are possible for (Eli, Fay), and we test each against both statements.
Knight–knight: Eli's sentence is true, since they are the same kind. But Fay, a knight, says that Eli is a knave, which is false. A knight has said something false, so this is a contradiction.
Knight–knave: Eli, a knight, says they are the same kind, but they differ, so his sentence is false. A knight has said something false.
Knave–knave: Eli is a knave, so his sentence would have to be false. Check it against this assignment.
Knave–knight: Eli is a knave and his sentence is false, as it must be, because the two differ. Fay is a knight and her sentence, “Eli is a knave”, is true. Nobody breaks a rule.
Exactly one assignment is left, so it is the answer.
workedSteps.math: Eli is a knave and Fay is a knight

reveal.text: Ada's sentence leaves two assignments: Ada a knight and Ben a knave, or Ada a knave and Ben a knight. Ben's sentence rules out the first, because there Ben would be a knave saying something true, that the two of them are different kinds.

lead.text: Sometimes the list ends up empty. Suppose an islander says, “I am a knave.” If she is a knight, her sentence is true, so she is a knave, which is a [[contradiction|A case that forces a claim to be both true and false, so it is ruled out. Met earlier in this lesson.]] with her being a knight. If she is a knave, her sentence is true, since she is one, and a knave never says anything true. Either way something goes wrong, and no assignment survives.

What this tells us is that *nobody* on the island can say that sentence. A puzzle that leaves nothing standing hasn't defeated the method, because **an empty list is the correct answer**: the statements cannot all have been made by knights and knaves.

lessons.orientation: Solving a small puzzle by assuming a case and following it until something breaks.
lessons.nextAction: Next, truth tables, which list every case at once.

blocks.text: In a knights and knaves puzzle, everyone on an island either always tells the truth or always lies, and what they say is your only evidence about which. If one of them says “I always tell the truth”, you learn nothing, because a truth-teller would say it truthfully and a liar would say it falsely.
The method for working it out is to suppose a case and follow it until it either holds up or breaks, which is the move mathematicians use to show that something is impossible.

intro.promise: By the end you'll solve a small knights and knaves puzzle by trying each case and ruling out the ones that break a rule.
intro.whyItMatters: Supposing a case and following it until something breaks is how mathematicians prove things, and it works on any argument.

recap.keyIdea: To solve a knights and knaves puzzle, list every assignment, rule out each one that makes someone break the rule for their kind, and see what is left.

blocks.text: A **knight** says only true things and a **knave** only false ones, so each statement can be tested against each **assignment** of kinds. An assignment that makes a knight say something false, or a knave something true, ends in a **contradiction** and is ruled out. The puzzle is solved when exactly one assignment survives, and if none does, the statements could not all have been made, which is an answer in itself.

recap.nextHook: Next we make this listing of cases systematic, in the form of the truth table.

lessons.title: Building a truth table

lead.text: Let p be “Lamp 1 is on” and q be “Lamp 2 is on”. We make a column for each claim and a row for each state, and we take the states in a fixed order, with p changing slowest, so that none is missed or counted twice. The last column holds the verdict of the notice, the [[conditional|An if-then claim, p → q. It is false only when p is true and q is false. Met in 'If-then claims'.]] “If lamp 1 is on, lamp 2 is on”, in each state.

afterFigure.text: A table of this kind, with a row for every combination of true and false and a column for the value of a sentence, is a **truth table**. The notice is broken in *exactly one* row, the one in which lamp 1 is on and lamp 2 is off. **Every possible state is in the table**, so we can be sure that no other state breaks the notice.

diagram.outputLabel: If lamp 1 is on, lamp 2 is on

reveal.text: Only the first row, with p and q both true, gives “p and q” a true value. In each of the other three rows at least one of the two claims fails, and that is enough to make it false.

lead.text: In each row p and q have definite values, and a sentence made from them has a value that depends on nothing else. A common way of joining two claims is with “and”, which we write as ∧, so that p ∧ q reads “p and q”, and **p ∧ q is true in a row only when p is true and q is true there**.
We never needed to know what p and q were about, because the rule for ∧ looks only at the truth values in the row, and that is why one table can serve for every pair of claims.

A sign that offers “tea or coffee” would not be broken by someone who took both, whereas a menu offering “soup or salad” is usually meant to rule out taking both. The first reading, in which both is allowed, is called the **inclusive or**, and the second, in which both is ruled out, is the exclusive or.

afterFigure.text: Logic fixes on the inclusive reading and writes it ∨, so that p ∨ q is true in every row where at least one of p and q is true, and **false only when both are false**. If the exclusive meaning is intended, we say so in so many words, as in “p or q but not both”.

diagram.caption: The two readings differ only in the row where both are taken. Logic uses the inclusive one.

reveal.text: The only row that fails is the one with p true and q false, where ¬p and q are both false. Every other row has at least one true side, and the inclusive “or” needs only one.

lead.text: Each row of a table is one way the world might be. Every fact we are told rules out the rows in which it is false, so we cross those out and keep only the rows that fit everything we know. The figure steps through an example in which we are told that “p and q” is false, and then that p is true.

afterFigure.text: Once the facts have done their work, the rows still standing are all the ways the world could be, given what we know. **A conclusion follows only if it is true in every one of them**, and if even a *single* surviving row makes it false, then the facts do not force it. In the example one row is left, with q false, so q must be false.

steps.headline: Given p or q, and that p is false, must q be true?

lead.text: Here is the table method used on a small argument, with the facts applied one at a time.

workedSteps.text: We are told that p ∨ q is true and that p is false, and we ask whether q must be true. Write each row with p's value first, so that TF means p true and q false, and begin with all four.
The first fact is that p ∨ q is true. It is false only when both claims are false, so the last row goes and the other three stay.
The second fact is that p is false. Apply it to the three rows that are left, and only one of them survives.
One row is left, and in it q is true. No row that fits the facts has q false, so the conclusion follows.

blocks.text: Take the notice “If lamp 1 is on, lamp 2 is on”, which is about two lamps that can each be on or off. Looking at the lamps tells you whether the notice is being obeyed now, but not what it permits, and for that you need every state in front of you, with the notice's verdict beside each one.
A list of that kind can be made for any two claims, and it can also test a piece of reasoning.

intro.whyItMatters: A table of every case leaves nothing to judgment, so it settles whether a conclusion follows and shows where it fails.

recap.keyIdea: A truth table lists every case for the claims involved, and the rows that fit the known facts decide whether a conclusion follows.

blocks.text: A **truth table** has a row for every combination of true and false, so two claims need four rows and each further claim doubles them. In each row the value of a sentence such as p ∧ q, true only when both hold, or the inclusive p ∨ q, false only when both fail, depends on that row alone. To test reasoning we keep the rows that fit the facts, and the conclusion follows *only if* it holds in every one of them.

lessons.title: Finding the conclusion

lead.text: One [[claim|A sentence that says how things are, so it can turn out to be wrong. Met in 'What logic operates on'.]] is set apart as the one the speaker wants you to accept, and the others are offered to get you there. We call the claim to be accepted the **conclusion**, each claim offered in support of it a **premise**, and a conclusion together with its premises an **argument**. In the ferry example the conclusion is that the ferry won't run.

afterFigure.text: The word “argument” does not mean a quarrel here, and a premise is not necessarily true either; it is simply what is *offered*. **Finding the conclusion comes first**, because every other question about an argument depends on knowing what it is supposed to show.

reveal.text: The first two sentences are the support, and “therefore” introduces what they are meant to establish.

lead.text: Speakers often leave signals about which claim is which. Words such as “so”, “therefore”, “thus” and “hence” usually introduce a conclusion, and words such as “because”, “since” and “for” usually introduce a premise. We call them **indicator words**, and in the ferry example the “because” tells us that what follows it is a reason.

They are clues and no more. “Since” can also mean “from the time that”, as in “It has rained since Monday”, and plenty of arguments contain no indicator word at all. When the words don't settle it, ask the question that never fails: *which claim is the speaker trying to get me to accept, and which are there to help?*

It is natural to expect the conclusion to come last, because that is where we put it when we prove something. In ordinary speech it comes *wherever* the speaker finds convenient. A speaker will often begin with what they want you to accept and give the reasons afterwards, as in “You should take an umbrella. The forecast says rain, and you will be outside all afternoon.”

That passage has no indicator word, and its conclusion is the first sentence. We found it by asking what the other sentences are there to support, and that is the test to trust: **ask what each claim is doing for the others**.

steps.headline: “We must leave now, because the station is a long walk away and the last train is at nine”

lead.text: Here is a passage in which the conclusion comes first and a premise comes last, worked from the question of what each claim is doing.

workedSteps.text: Begin with what the speaker wants you to accept. Of the three claims, one tells us what to do, and the other two are facts of the kind that might explain why.
The other two claims, that the station is a long walk away and that the last train is at nine, do not ask anything of us, so neither of them is the one the speaker wants us to accept.
workedSteps.math: Premises: the station is a long walk away; the last train is at nine

workedSteps.text: Check by putting “so” in the right place: the station is a long walk away and the last train is at nine, so we must leave now. It reads naturally, and the other order would not.

The torch argument becomes the [[conditional|An if-then claim, p → q. It is false only when p is true and q is false. Met in 'If-then claims'.]] p → q, and p, and therefore q: **two premises and a conclusion**.

Met in 'Building a truth table'.]] is then ready to use. The rows in which *every premise is true* are the cases where all of the speaker's reasons hold, and finding those rows is the first step in testing an argument.

blocks.text: Here is a short piece of reasoning: “The ferry won't run today, because the wind is above gale force and the company cancels the ferry in a gale.” It joins three claims, and one is the claim the speaker wants us to accept, while the other two are there to persuade us of it.
Seeing this is what makes it possible to ask whether reasoning is any good, because until we know what is being supported there is nothing to assess.

intro.promise: By the end you'll pick out an argument's conclusion however it is worded, and find the rows where its premises all hold.
intro.whyItMatters: You can't ask whether an argument is any good until you know what it is trying to prove.

recap.keyIdea: The conclusion is the claim an argument wants you to accept, and its premises are the claims offered to support it, whatever order they come in.

blocks.text: An **argument** is a **conclusion** together with the **premises** offered in support of it. Words like “so” and “because” are useful clues but not proof, and a claim's position tells us nothing, so the test is to ask which claim the others are *there to support*. Written in letters, the torch argument shows how a truth table can find the rows in which every premise is true.

recap.nextHook: Next we ask whether the premises of an argument really do support its conclusion, and, separately, whether they are true.

lessons.title: Valid but untrue

lead.text: The first question a logician asks about an argument is not whether its [[premises|Claims offered in support of a conclusion. Met in 'Finding the conclusion'.]] are true but whether its [[conclusion|The claim an argument wants you to accept. Met in 'Finding the conclusion'.]] *follows* from them. To find out, grant the premises of the whale argument for a moment: suppose that every mammal lives on land, and that whales are mammals. Could whales then live anywhere else? They couldn't, since a whale would be a mammal and every mammal would live on land. When the conclusion is forced in this way we call the argument **valid**: there is no way for all of its premises to be true while its conclusion is false.

afterFigure.text: Validity is a claim about how the premises and the conclusion are *connected*, and it says nothing about whether any of them is true. That is why we could judge the whale argument without knowing anything about whales, and why a valid argument can have a false premise and a false conclusion, as this one does. The reverse holds too: an argument whose premises and conclusion all happen to be true is not thereby valid, because **validity asks what must be so, not what happens to be so**.

reveal.text: The only row in which both premises are true is the first, with p and q both true, and q is true there. No row has true premises and a false conclusion.

lead.text: Strip an argument down to letters, so that the particular claims no longer matter, and what remains is its **pattern**. A pattern is valid exactly when its conclusion is **true in every row in which all its premises are true**. In the pattern “p ∧ q; therefore q”, the only row in which the premise is true has p and q both true, and q is true there, so the pattern is valid.

afterFigure.text: A valid pattern works whatever claims are put in place of the letters, which is why we can test the pattern once and trust every argument that has its shape.

lead.text: Now the other side of the test. Suppose some row makes every premise true and the conclusion false. That row is a way things could be in which all the reasons hold and the claim they are meant to support fails, and we call it a **counterexample** to the argument. An argument that has a counterexample is invalid, which just means that it is not valid.

One counterexample is *enough*, because validity is a promise about *every* case, and a single exception breaks it. So while you are testing you can stop the moment you find such a row, whereas you can only call the pattern valid after **every** row with true premises has been checked.
Here is a pattern that has the look of good reasoning, tested row by row.

workedSteps.text: Write the four rows, with p's value first, so that TF means p true and q false.
Keep the rows in which both premises are true. The premise p ∨ q fails only in the last row, and the premise q fails in the second and the last, so two rows remain.
Now look at the conclusion, p, in each of those rows. It is true in TT but false in FT, so FT has true premises and a false conclusion. That row is a counterexample.
The pattern is invalid, however well it seems to behave in the other rows.

reveal.text: In the row with p false and q true, p → q is true because its antecedent is false, q is true, and the conclusion p is false. That row is a counterexample, and it is the same row that told a conditional apart from its converse.

lead.text: We call an argument **sound** when it is valid and every one of its premises is true. Validity carries the truth of the premises across to the conclusion, so the conclusion of a sound argument is guaranteed to be true. The whale argument is valid but not sound, since its first premise is false.

afterFigure.text: An argument can therefore go wrong in two separate ways. It can be invalid, so that its conclusion doesn't follow even if everything it says is *granted*, or it can be valid but unsound, so that the reasoning is fine but it starts from something false. When you meet a conclusion you believe to be false, ask which has happened, and if you know the argument is valid, **one of its premises must be false**.

Only the cell where the argument is valid and every premise is true is sound, and it guarantees a true conclusion. A valid argument with a false premise is unsound and guarantees nothing. An invalid argument gives no guarantee either way.

lessons.orientation: Judging whether a conclusion follows, separately from whether the premises are true.
lessons.nextAction: Next, the common fallacies of if-then reasoning.

blocks.text: Here is an argument: all mammals live on land; whales are mammals; therefore whales live on land. Is it a good argument? Most people say no at once, because the conclusion is plainly false, and yet a logician would tell you that the reasoning in it is faultless. The disagreement comes from two different questions that everyday speech runs together: whether the conclusion follows from the premises, and whether the premises are true.
Keeping the two apart tells you what to challenge when you meet a conclusion you reject, the reasoning or one of the reasons.

intro.promise: By the end you'll test whether a conclusion follows, find the case that refutes it, and judge separately whether the premises are true.
intro.whyItMatters: A conclusion can be false because the reasoning is bad or because a premise is, and knowing which tells you what to challenge.

recap.keyIdea: An argument is valid when its conclusion must be true if its premises are, and sound when it is valid and its premises really are true.

blocks.text: We call an argument **valid** when no row of the table makes every premise true and the conclusion false, and a single such row, a **counterexample**, is enough to show it invalid. We call it **sound** when it is valid *and* every premise is true, so a sound argument guarantees its conclusion. When you assess an argument, ask the two questions separately: does the conclusion follow, and are the premises true?

recap.nextHook: Next we use the test to name the two patterns of if-then reasoning that persuade without supporting, and the one that does.

lessons.title: Naming the fallacies

lead.text: Take the rule “If it rains, the street is wet”, which we can write as p → q, with p for “It rains” and q for “The street is wet”. It does not say that p is the *only* way to reach q: a street can be wet because a cleaner has just been along it, or because a pipe has burst, and neither of those makes the rule false.

afterFigure.text: So when we find the street wet, we are looking at the consequent and trying to run the rule backwards, from q to p, which is the move the [[converse|The conditional with its parts swapped: q → p. Met in 'Converse and contrapositive'.]] invites. **What the rule gives us is a route from rain to a wet street, and nothing about the way back.**

lead.text: The pattern we have just been tempted by is “p → q; q; therefore p”. Its second premise asserts, or *affirms*, the consequent q, and from that it concludes the antecedent p, so we call it **affirming the consequent**. It is invalid, as the test of the last lesson will show in a moment, and it belongs to a larger family. A pattern of reasoning that persuades without really supporting its conclusion is a **fallacy**.
It persuades because the rule seems to fit the situation so neatly: the street is wet, which is just what the rule says rain would produce. But fitting is not the same as following.

reveal.text: In the row with p false and q true, the street is wet because the cleaner has been, so the rule holds, the second premise holds, and it did not rain.

lead.text: There is a second pattern that looks equally natural: “p → q; ¬p; therefore ¬q”. It didn't rain, so the street isn't wet. This time the second premise denies the antecedent, and we call the pattern **denying the antecedent**. It fails for the *same* reason as before, since the rule never said that rain is the only cause.

Negating both parts of a conditional without swapping them gives ¬p → ¬q, which is neither the converse nor the [[contrapositive|The conditional with its parts swapped and both negated: ¬q → ¬p. It says the same as the original. Met in 'Converse and contrapositive'.]] of the rule, and denying the antecedent treats that different claim as though it followed from the rule.

There is a way of arguing backwards from a rule that cannot go wrong. If the street is dry, it did not rain, because rain would have made it wet. In letters this is “p → q; ¬q; therefore ¬p”: the rule, the denial of its consequent, and the denial of its antecedent. If p were true, the rule would force q, and q is false, so p *cannot* be true.

This is the contrapositive at work, and it is called **modus tollens**, from the Latin for “the mode that denies”. Its better-known sibling is “p → q; p; therefore q”, which reasons forwards from the condition and is called modus ponens. Both are valid, and the two fallacies are what you get by running them the wrong way round: **affirming the consequent and denying the antecedent are modus ponens and modus tollens turned back to front**.

steps.headline: If the sensor overheats its light comes on, and the light is off

lead.text: Here is the safe direction used on a rule you can picture, with each step of the supposing written out.

workedSteps.text: Take the rule “If the sensor overheats, its warning light comes on”, and suppose we find the light off. Now suppose, just for a moment, that the sensor had overheated, and ask what the rule would say about the light.
That supposition clashes with what we see, so it cannot be right, and the sensor did not overheat.
In letters, with p for overheating and q for the light being on, we started from the rule and the denial of its consequent, and ended with the denial of its antecedent.

reveal.text: The only row in which both ¬q → ¬p and p are true is the one with p true and q true, and q is true there. There is no counterexample, because ¬q → ¬p is the contrapositive of p → q and says the same thing, so this is modus ponens in another form.

lead.text: Some fallacies can't be caught by a truth table, because what goes wrong is the topic. Take “Their report on the bridge must be wrong, because they are arrogant.” The conclusion is about a report, and the premise is about the person who wrote it, so the premise gives no reason at all to accept the conclusion. We call this **attacking the person**.

To answer an argument, examine its reasoning: look for a premise that is false, a step that doesn't follow, or a premise that has been left out. The character of the speaker matters only when the claim is *about* the speaker, as when we ask whether a witness was in the room.

lessons.orientation: Naming the two invalid patterns of if-then reasoning, and the valid one beside them.
lessons.nextAction: Try the changed cases in your review queue.

blocks.text: Here is a rule that nobody doubts: if it has rained, the street is wet. A wet street seems to suggest that it rained, and a dry street seems to suggest that it didn't, and the two look equally sensible, yet one of them is safe and the other is not.
Reasoning from an if-then rule goes wrong in a few recognisable ways, and each way has a name.

intro.promise: By the end you'll name the two common fallacies of if-then reasoning, refute each with one row, and spot the valid pattern beside them.
intro.whyItMatters: These patterns turn up in everyday arguments, and naming them lets you say exactly what has gone wrong.

recap.keyIdea: Reasoning from q back to p, or from not-p to not-q, is invalid, while reasoning from not-q to not-p is valid.

blocks.text: A **fallacy** is a pattern of reasoning that persuades without supporting. Of the four ways of using “p → q; …”, two are fallacies, **affirming the consequent** and **denying the antecedent**, and each has a counterexample in the row where p is false and q is true. The other two are valid, and **modus tollens**, which runs from ¬q to ¬p, is the contrapositive at work. Fallacies such as **attacking the person** change the subject, and the answer to them is to examine the reasoning.

recap.nextHook: The next time you meet an argument, find its conclusion first, then ask the two questions: does it follow, and are the premises true?

questions.prompt: Which of these sentences is a claim?
hints: Which sentence could someone check and find wrong?
Compare a sentence that says how things are with one that asks and one that tells.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: “The kettle is boiling” says how things are, so it can be checked. A question asks and a command directs.

choices.label: Is the kettle boiling?
The kettle is boiling
Boil the kettle

questions.onCorrect: The kettle either is boiling or isn't, so the sentence can be wrong. The question asks and the command directs, and neither can be wrong.

misconceptions.feedback: That asks for information. It says nothing about the kettle, so there is nothing in it to find wrong.
That tells someone to act. It can be obeyed or ignored, but it can't be found wrong.

questions.prompt: The sentence “The envelope holds a £10 note” is about an envelope that is sealed, and nobody has opened it. Which of these is true of the sentence right now?
hints: Ask whether opening the envelope changes what is in it, or only what we know about it.
Is “unknown” something the envelope could show, or something you feel before looking?

acceptedIdeas: It is already true or already false, and opening the envelope will only show which.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The envelope already holds a note or it doesn't, so the sentence is already true or already false.

choices.label: It has a third value besides true and false, “unknown”, until someone opens the envelope.
It is neither true nor false until someone opens the envelope.
It is already true or already false, and opening the envelope will only show which.

questions.onCorrect: The envelope holds a note or it doesn't, and that already settles the sentence. Looking only tells us which.

misconceptions.feedback: Opening the envelope changes what we know, not the sentence. The envelope already holds a note or it doesn't, and that settles the sentence.
“Unknown” describes the person who hasn't looked, not the sentence. The sentence is true or false whatever anyone knows.

questions.prompt: p is “The soup is hot”, and the soup is cold. Is ¬p true or false? Answer with one word.
hints: Is “The soup is hot” true of cold soup?
¬p takes the opposite value to p.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: True: p is false, so ¬p is true.

questions.onCorrect: True. Cold soup makes p false, and ¬p, “The soup is not hot”, takes the opposite value.

misconceptions.feedback: ¬p says that the soup is not hot, and cold soup makes that sentence right.

questions.prompt: How should we treat “This painting is beautiful”?
hints: The speaker is saying how the painting is, even if others disagree.
Does the sentence ask for anything, or tell anyone to do anything?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It asserts an evaluation, so it is a claim, though people dispute it.

choices.label: As a question
As a command
As a disputed claim

questions.onCorrect: It puts forward a view about the painting, so it is a claim. Disagreement doesn't turn a claim into a question or a command.

misconceptions.feedback: Nobody is told to do anything. The speaker says how the painting is.
It asks for nothing. It states a view, which others may dispute.

questions.prompt: “Close the window.” Is that a claim, a question or a command? Answer with one word.
hints: Ask whether the sentence says how things are or directs someone to act.
The verb “Close” asks for an action.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is a command: it directs an action rather than asserting a truth.

questions.onCorrect: It directs an action and doesn't say how anything is, so it can't be true or false.

misconceptions.feedback: Could anyone find “Close the window” wrong? It tells someone what to do.
It asks for no information. It tells someone to act.

questions.prompt: A claim is false. Is its negation true or false? Answer with one word.
hints: Apply negation to the false claim.
Negation never leaves the value alone.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The negation of a false claim is true.

questions.onCorrect: True. Negation reverses the value, so the negation of a false claim is true.

misconceptions.feedback: Negation never leaves the value alone. Ask what ¬ does to a claim.

questions.prompt: Let p be “The door opens” and q be “The access code is correct”, so the lock's rule is q → p. Which case makes the rule false?
hints: Which letter now stands for the code, and which for the door?
The rule is broken only when the code is correct and the door stays shut.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: p false and q true: the code is right and the door stays shut.

choices.label: p false, q false
p false, q true
p true, q false

questions.onCorrect: With p for the door and q for the code, a right code and a shut door is p false with q true, the one case where the rule demands something and doesn't get it.

misconceptions.feedback: Here the door opens and the code is wrong, since p is now the door. The rule has no demand on the door to break when the code is wrong.
Here the code is wrong, since q is now the code. The rule only said something about correct codes.

questions.prompt: The rule is “If the kettle boils, it switches itself off.” The kettle hasn't boiled, and it switches off anyway because someone presses its switch. What does that do to the rule?
hints: Ask what the rule demands when the kettle hasn't boiled.
A rule is broken only when its condition holds and the result fails to follow.

acceptedIdeas: It does not break the rule, because the rule only says what happens when the kettle boils.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The rule only covers a kettle that boils, so switching off before that doesn't break it.

choices.label: It leaves the rule undecided, because the rule does not cover a kettle that hasn't boiled.
It does not break the rule, because the rule only says what happens when the kettle boils.
It breaks the rule, because the kettle switched off without boiling.

questions.onCorrect: The kettle never boiled, so the condition never arose and nothing the rule demands has failed. Here p is false and q is true, and p → q is true.

misconceptions.feedback: The rule never says the kettle stays on until it boils. It only says what happens when it boils, so switching off early contradicts nothing in it.
A conditional is always true or false. When its condition does not arise, nothing it demands has failed, and we count it as true.

questions.prompt: p is “The access code is correct” and q is “The door opens”, and both are false. Is p → q true or false? Answer with one word.
hints: Is the code correct in this case?
A rule about correct codes can't be broken by a wrong code.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: True: p is false, so the rule is not broken.

questions.onCorrect: True. With a wrong code the rule isn't tested, so nothing breaks it.

misconceptions.feedback: The rule only said something about correct codes. Does a wrong code with a shut door break that?

questions.prompt: p is “The shape is a square” and q is “The shape has four sides”. For a four-sided rectangle that isn't a square, is p → q true or false? Answer with one word.
hints: Is p true for this shape?
A rule about squares can't be broken by a shape that isn't one.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: True: p is false, so the conditional is not broken.

questions.onCorrect: True. The shape isn't a square, so the rule about squares is untouched. A true q doesn't make p true.

misconceptions.feedback: p is false for this shape. A rule about squares can't be broken by a shape that isn't one.

questions.prompt: p is true and q is false. Is p → q true or false? Answer with one word.
hints: Is the condition met in this case?
Does q deliver what p called for?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: False: p true with q false is the one breaking case.

questions.onCorrect: False. The antecedent holds and the consequent fails, the one case that breaks a conditional.

misconceptions.feedback: p holds, so the conditional is being tested. Does q deliver what p called for?

questions.prompt: Which of these is true of p → q?
hints: Go through the four combinations of p and q and mark the ones that break the rule.
Which combination asks something of the rule and doesn't get it?

acceptedIdeas: It is false in exactly one of the four combinations of p and q.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Only p true with q false makes it false.

choices.label: It is false whenever p and q have different truth values.
It is false in exactly one of the four combinations of p and q.
It is false whenever q is false.
It is false whenever p is false.

questions.onCorrect: Only p true with q false breaks it, so p → q is false in exactly one combination and true in the other three.

misconceptions.feedback: When p is false the rule's condition never arises, so p → q is true there, whatever q is.
With q false it is false only if p is true. When p is false as well, nothing is demanded of q, and p → q is true.
Different values include p false with q true, and p → q is true there. Only p true with q false breaks it.

questions.prompt: Let p be “The code is correct” and q be “The door opens”. In the row where p is false and q is true, p → q is true. Is q → p true or false in that row? Answer with one word.
hints: In q → p, which part is the antecedent?
Is q true and p false a case with a true antecedent and a false consequent?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: False: q → p has a true antecedent and a false consequent.

questions.onCorrect: False. In q → p the antecedent q holds and the consequent p fails. p → q is true in this same case.

misconceptions.feedback: In q → p, q comes first. Apply the rule from the last lesson with q as the antecedent.

questions.prompt: Compare p → q with its converse q → p in each of the four combinations of p and q. Which of these is true?
hints: Find the combination in which each claim is false.
Each claim is false in exactly one combination. Is it the same one?

acceptedIdeas: They take different truth values in exactly two combinations.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: They differ when p is true and q is false, and when p is false and q is true.

choices.label: They take the same truth value in every combination.
They take different truth values in exactly two combinations.
They take different truth values in exactly one combination.

questions.onCorrect: p → q is false only when p is true and q is false, and q → p only when p is false and q is true, so the two differ in both of those rows and agree in the other two.

misconceptions.feedback: That is true of the contrapositive. The converse is false in a different row from p → q, so the two must come apart somewhere.
The row with p false and q true is one place they differ. Check the row with p true and q false as well.

questions.prompt: Which case makes p → q true but its converse q → p false?
hints: The converse is false only when q is true and p is false.
Check that p → q is still true in that case.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: With p false and q true, p → q is true and q → p is false.

choices.label: p true, q false
p true, q true
p false, q true

questions.onCorrect: p false, q true. The original holds, the converse fails, so the two are not the same claim.

misconceptions.feedback: Both are true here. You need a case where they disagree.
Here p → q is already false. You need it true.

questions.prompt: Choose the contrapositive of “If a parcel is fragile, it is labelled”.
hints: Swap the parts, then negate both.
The new antecedent is the negation of the old consequent.

acceptedIdeas: If a parcel is not labelled, it is not fragile.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: If a parcel is not labelled, it is not fragile.

choices.label: If a parcel is not labelled, it is not fragile.
If a parcel is labelled, it is fragile.
If a parcel is not fragile, it is not labelled.

questions.onCorrect: Swap the parts and negate both: if a parcel is not labelled, it is not fragile. It says the same as the original.

misconceptions.feedback: That swaps the parts but doesn't negate them. It is the converse.
That negates both parts but keeps the order. It isn't the contrapositive.

questions.prompt: Relative to p → q, what is q → p called? Answer with one word.
hints: It swaps the two parts and negates nothing.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The converse.

questions.onCorrect: The converse. The parts are swapped and nothing is negated.

misconceptions.feedback: The contrapositive also negates both parts. Here they are only swapped.

questions.prompt: Relative to p → q, what is ¬q → ¬p called? Answer with one word.
hints: The parts are swapped and both are negated.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The contrapositive.

questions.onCorrect: The contrapositive. The parts are swapped and both are negated.

misconceptions.feedback: The converse only swaps the parts. Here both are negated as well.

questions.prompt: Ada says, “Ben is a knave.” If Ada is a knight, is Ben a knight or a knave? Answer with one word.
hints: A knight's sentence is true.
If it is true that Ben is a knave, what is Ben?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Ben is a knave, because a knight's statement is true.

questions.onCorrect: Knave. A knight's sentence is true, so Ada's claim about Ben has to hold.

misconceptions.feedback: Ada says Ben is a knave. If Ada always tells the truth, what does that make Ben?

hints: Test the four assignments one at a time against what Ada says.
If Ada is a knight, her sentence must be true. If she is a knave, it must be false.

acceptedIdeas: Ada and Ben are different kinds, in either order.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Ada a knight with Ben a knave fits, and Ada a knave with Ben a knight fits. The other two assignments do not.

choices.label: Only the assignment in which Ada is a knight and Ben is a knave.
Ada and Ben are the same kind, both knights or both knaves.
Ada and Ben are different kinds, in either order.

questions.onCorrect: A knight Ada needs Ben to be a knave, and a knave Ada needs Ben to be a knight, so the two mixed pairs survive.

That assignment fits, but so does the one where Ada is a knave and Ben is a knight, because her sentence is then false, as a knave's must be.

questions.prompt: Ada says, “Ben is a knave,” and Ben says, “Ada and I are different kinds.” Is Ada a knight or a knave? Answer with one word.
hints: Ada's sentence leaves two assignments. Test Ben's sentence against each.
In the assignment where Ada is a knight, Ben is a knave. Is his sentence false, as a knave's must be?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Ada is a knave and Ben a knight.

questions.onCorrect: Knave. Ben's sentence is true in both assignments that Ada's sentence leaves, so he can't be the knave, and Ada is.
